plot_extraction.response_text:
The lecherous Duke of Orleans becomes obsessed with Bertha, the beautiful and steadfastly virtuous wife of his loyal follower Raoul d’Hocquetonville. After she rejects him, he traps her in the queen’s chambers, but she threatens suicide rather than submit. Seeking revenge, the duke secretly confines her in a dark bedroom, invites Raoul and several companions to a drunken supper, and persuades Raoul that an exceptionally skilled courtesan awaits him nearby. Unable to reveal herself without risking disgrace, Bertha is forced into an encounter with her own husband, who remains unaware of her identity.

Humiliated and emotionally devastated, Bertha warns the duke that his scheme will cost them all dearly. Raoul later leaves the duke’s service for that of the Duke of Burgundy and, after learning the truth, kills the Duke of Orleans with a club. Bertha dies young within the year, while Raoul mourns her deeply. The tragedy presents the duke’s death as the eventual price of his cruelty and abuse of two honorable people.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the manner of a late-medieval chronicle retold through a consciously antiquarian, nineteenth-century voice. It presents scandalous court history as though recovering a suppressed anecdote, surrounding the central episode with genealogical details, historical names, dates, locations, epitaphs, and references to other collections of tales. This documentary scaffolding gives the narrative mock authority, while the narrator’s partiality, exaggeration, and delight in gossip continually undermine any appearance of sober historiography. The result is a pseudo-historical fabliau: a tragic sexual intrigue narrated with the expansive energy of a bawdy fireside tale.

The narrator is highly intrusive, conversational, and performative. He addresses the reader indirectly, pauses to comment on national character and human folly, interprets motives, passes moral judgments, and openly controls the transition into the tale with phrases such as “But now for mine.” His stance is unstable by design. At first he appears amused by aristocratic libertinism and celebrates youth, wine, sensuality, and merriment; later, as the duke’s conduct becomes coercive and destructive, the narration condemns him as wicked, disloyal, diabolical, and villainous. This shifting perspective creates a tension between relish in the telling and horror at what is told. The voice is worldly and cynical, yet ultimately affirms fidelity, innocence, and moral consequence.

The prose is ornate, exuberant, and accumulative. Sentences are often long and syntactically layered, using subordinate clauses, parenthetical historical explanations, parallel constructions, and extended catalogues. Lists are a signature device: forms of hunting, varieties of sexual behaviour, classes of disreputable women, courtly luxuries, and methods of temptation are piled up until they become comic through excess. Repetition and amplification repeatedly turn a simple assertion into a rhetorical performance. Short exclamations and abrupt statements—“I am undone!”, “Never, while I live,” or “Ha! Ha! Ha!”—punctuate these elaborate periods, sharpening moments of danger or theatrical confrontation.

The diction mixes archaism, courtly refinement, earthy insult, and euphemistic obscenity. Titles, saints’ oaths, formal modes of address, old-fashioned inversions, and expressions such as “said lady,” “my lord and master,” and “thereupon” sustain the historical illusion. Alongside them appear vigorous colloquialisms such as “rapscallion,” “muckworms,” “hussies,” and “tarred with the same brush.” Sexual acts are rarely described in direct anatomical language; instead, they are elaborated through metaphors of feasting, riding, hunting, warfare, religion, jewellery, confectionery, and paradise. This figurative indirection allows the prose to be simultaneously decorous and lewd. Occasional grammatical awkwardness and unusual phrasing contribute to the impression of an older work mediated through antiquated translation.

Figurative language is abundant and deliberately extravagant. Beauty is expressed through flowers, radiance, whiteness, and heavenly gifts; lust becomes fever, fire, appetite, sport, or horsemanship; corruption appears as mud, poison, worms, and suffocation. The duke’s seduction speech develops sensual images in arabesque profusion, while the lady’s decline is compressed into the melancholy image of “a flower deprived of air and eaten by a worm.” Comic comparisons are often grotesquely incongruous, as when abstract social claims are illustrated through oysters’ plumage or birds’ shells. Such images cultivate a Rabelaisian atmosphere in which bodily appetite, verbal invention, and moral satire are inseparable.

Dialogue is lengthy, rhetorical, and strongly differentiated by moral position. The Lady d’Hocquetonville speaks in balanced, principled arguments centred on children, reputation, marriage, age, and enduring affection. Her language is formal and controlled even under threat, making speech her first weapon before she turns to the stiletto. The duke speaks through wit, sophistry, teasing obscenity, threats, and seductive verbal abundance. Raoul’s initial dialogue establishes him as loyal and domestically virtuous, which heightens the cruelty of the trap. Conversations therefore do more than convey information: they stage contests between chastity and appetite, integrity and manipulation, self-command and intoxication.

The narrative structure is linear but heavily framed. A discursive opening introduces the duke’s reputation and the supposed history of the anecdote; the central action then proceeds through temptation, entrapment, banquet, deception, and violation; a compressed aftermath records murder, death, burial, and retrospective judgment. Suspense depends on dramatic irony. The imprisoned wife hears her husband being coaxed toward the adjoining room, while he remains unaware of her identity; the reader understands the duke’s scheme before Raoul does. Repeated thresholds—the marked floorboard, the locked chamber, the secret door, and the garden exit—give the episode a claustrophobic theatricality. The banquet scene slows time through speeches and drinking, prolonging the wife’s dread before the catastrophe.

Tonally, the story combines farce, erotic comedy, melodrama, moral exemplum, and tragedy. The opening boasts, sexual metaphors, drinking scene, and masculine banter belong to comic fabliau, but the coerced situation and fatal aftermath expose the violence beneath courtly gallantry. Laughter is especially double-edged: it signals sociability and verbal pleasure, yet also the duke’s cruelty and the courtiers’ loss of shame. The closing movement replaces exuberance with elegiac gravity, using the tomb inscription and Burgundy’s melancholy reflection to recast the anecdote as the destruction of two honourable lives.

The central thematic contrast is between appetite without restraint and virtue placed under intolerable pressure. Other recurring concerns include the abuse of aristocratic power, male complicity, the fragility of reputation, the corrupting effects of wine and group behaviour, marital fidelity, and the delayed but inevitable cost of private wrongdoing. The final maxim universalises the episode into a lesson about folly and retribution, though its claim that “there is a woman at the bottom of everything” retains the narrator’s characteristic mixture of proverb, irony, misogynistic convention, and historical fatalism. Overall, the style is sensuous, digressive, mock-scholarly, theatrically rhetorical, and morally ambivalent: it revels in bawdy invention while finally condemning the cruelty that such libertinism can conceal.

### THE DARK CHAMBER OF THE HÔTEL BARBETTE

Among the many adventures of Louis, Duke of Orleans, brother to King Charles the Sixth of France, there is one which certain discreet chroniclers have passed over as a cat passes a hot porringer—looking another way, yet smelling the meat all the while. Monstrelet says nothing of it; Juvenal des Ursins says less; the anonymous clerk of Saint-Denis, who knew the weight of a crown and the price of parchment, gives but three crooked lines, since scraped away by some pious hand. Nevertheless, the tale was preserved in the house of Hocquetonville, and afterward repeated at Lille by old Madame de Croy, who had it from her grandmother’s confessor, whose uncle had served the Duke of Burgundy in the year of the great frost. This is sufficient authority for a scandal; indeed, twice as much as scandals commonly possess.

Louis of Orleans was then the brightest, boldest, best-hosed, worst-governed prince in Christendom. He hunted stag in the forest, boar in the marsh, heron by the river, wenches in the town, ladies at court, widows after vespers, and reputations wherever honest husbands had stored them. He loved hawks with wide wings, horses with narrow flanks, wines without water, suppers without reckoning, and women without scruples—though, to do him justice, he preferred them with scruples, for resistance whetted him as vinegar sharpens an onion.

He had pages to carry his gloves, equerries to hold his stirrup, musicians to tune his sleep, astrologers to excuse his follies, physicians to repair them, priests to absolve them, and flatterers to persuade him they were virtues. Gold ran through his fingers like rain through a gargoyle’s mouth. His hôtel was a fair of silks, spices, lapdogs, lutes, peacock pies, silver cups, perfumed baths, velvet cushions, Italian sweetmeats, Spanish leather, Flemish tapestry, German steel, and those painted hussies who came from nowhere, belonged to nobody, and knew everybody.

Now there are men who, having eaten enough, cease eating; others, having drunk enough, fall under the board and thereby offend no more until morning. But lust is a pantry without a door, a barrel without a bottom, a creditor who doubles the account whenever he is paid. The duke, having tasted every easy pleasure, began to hunger after the difficult; and as a child who has a basket of apples cries for the one upon the church wall, so his Grace coveted most fiercely those ladies who belonged by honour, affection, law, habit, children, sacrament, and common sense to other men.

At that time there served him a knight called Raoul d’Hocquetonville, descended, according to the family roll, from Hugues the Iron-Bearded, who accompanied Count Robert upon some crusade which the count himself never made. Raoul was not rich, but of good lineage; not subtle, but of good faith; not eloquent, but of good courage. He rode straight, struck hard, paid his debts when able, and when unable confessed them without inventing a Jew, a flood, a fire, or a sick aunt in Picardy. Such men are rarer in courts than white ravens, feathered oysters, or lawyers who shorten a lawsuit.

Raoul had married Bertha de Montfaucon, called by those who saw her Bertha the Fair, though beauty was the least valuable of her possessions. Her hair was of that brown which takes fire in sunlight; her brow smooth and broad; her eyes grey, clear, and steady; her mouth neither too grave for kindness nor too merry for prudence. She was not one of your sugar saints, pale from vanity and devout from indigestion, but a woman of warm blood, sound understanding, and firm affection. She bore Raoul two children, tended his old mother, ordered his household, remembered his tenants’ names, and loved her husband after seven years of marriage—which last accomplishment should have placed her among the miracles of Saint Denis.

The duke first saw her at a Christmas entertainment given by the queen. Bertha wore blue damask bordered with miniver, no jewels except a little cross, and no paint except the colour that rose when she laughed. She spoke little, danced once with her husband, and left before the masks became insolent. From that evening Louis carried her image as a fever carries heat.

He questioned Raoul concerning her, praising first her gown, then her manners, then her wit, and last her beauty, as one who walks round a fortress seeking the weakest gate.

“My lord,” said Raoul, smiling, “you honour my poor house. Bertha is better than I deserve.”

“Then lend me thy fortune, Hocquetonville.”

“All that I have is yours, saving my wife and my salvation.”

The duke laughed.

“Keep the latter; it is a lean possession. As for the former, guard it well.”

Raoul, hearing only jest where malice had already laid its eggs, laughed likewise. Thus do honest men often ring the bell for their own calamity.

The duke began with courtesies: flowers from his gardens, fruits from the south, a little book of prayers illuminated in gold, a cage of linnets, a mirror from Venice, and a length of cloth so delicate that, as his messenger declared, it might be drawn through a wedding ring. Bertha returned the jewels, gave the birds to a convent, sent the fruit to the sick, covered the mirror, kept the prayer book because sacred words are not dishonoured by profane intentions, and had the cloth cut into altar veils.

This amused the duke prodigiously.

“She makes ladders of my arrows,” said he. “By Saint Cupid, I shall climb them!”

Then came letters, those paper ferrets which princes thrust into every domestic hole. In one he called her the rose of Valois, the moon of Paris, the pearl in Raoul’s wooden cup, the white hind of his forest, the key of his paradise, and the sole physician capable of curing the wound she had made. Bertha burned it. In another he compared himself to Leander, Paris, Lancelot, Tristan, Pyramus, and King Solomon, thereby confessing more sins than examples. That she burned also.

At length he met her in a gallery of the queen’s apartments, where she waited upon a kinswoman. The gallery looked upon the royal garden, and the snow outside made the winter sun so bright that every flaw in a man’s face—and sometimes in his soul—seemed plainly visible.

“Madame d’Hocquetonville,” said the duke, barring her passage with the grace of a dancing master and the authority of a gaoler, “you treat my devotion cruelly.”

“My lord, I treat it as it deserves.”

“You have not read my letters.”

“I have read enough to know they should be burned.”

“Fire is the proper altar for love.”

“It is also the proper end of corruption.”

“Ha! A thrust! Raoul has married a swordsman in petticoats.”

“Raoul has married a wife, my lord. Remember that word.”

The duke leaned nearer. He was handsome when he wished to be, and terrible when handsome, for beauty in a powerful wicked man is a gilded handle upon a poisoned blade.

“Words,” said he, “are little fences built by frightened gardeners. Love leaps them. Consider, sweet lady, how short is youth. Spring hastens, roses fall, snow invades the hair, teeth desert the mouth, and the eyes which now command kingdoms must one day bargain with spectacles. Why hoard treasure for the worms? Let us drink while the cup is warm. I offer you secrecy, splendour, tenderness, palaces—”

“You offer me shame.”

“A name given by old women to pleasures they can no longer enjoy.”

“I have children.”

“They shall be enriched.”

“I have a husband.”

“He shall be advanced.”

“I have honour.”

“I shall worship it.”

“You have already insulted it.”

Then Louis changed his instrument, as a musician who, failing with the lute, takes up the trumpet.

“You speak boldly to your prince.”

“I speak faithfully to my husband.”

“Your husband is my servant.”

“And therefore doubly under your protection.”

This answer struck him, but did not cure him. Vice seldom lacks ears; it lacks obedience to what enters them.

“Madame,” said he, lowering his voice, “there are doors at court which open to a whisper and close upon a cry.”

“And there are windows, my lord, through which an honest woman may escape a dishonourable prince.”

She left him standing beneath the painted histories of Lucretia and Susanna, which, had he looked upward, might have preached what no confessor had yet persuaded him to hear.

For some weeks he ceased his pursuit, and Bertha hoped the storm had passed. Alas! A prince’s silence is often not peace but carpentry: he is building the trap.

In February, when the queen lay at the Hôtel Barbette, Bertha was summoned to attend her. The message bore the queen’s seal, or an imitation so good that the devil himself might have kissed it. She came at dusk, passed through the outer court, ascended the stair, and was led by a chamberwoman whom she did not know into a room hung with green tapestry.

“The queen will presently receive you,” said the woman, and withdrew.

Bertha waited. Presently the duke entered.

She rose so quickly that her chair fell.

“My lord!”

“My lady.”

“This is infamous.”

“This is private.”

He turned the key.

The chamber was richly furnished: a fire of applewood, candles in silver branches, wine warmed with cinnamon, preserved quinces, a low couch spread with cloth of gold, and upon the floor fresh rushes scented with lavender. What splendour! What comfort! What excellent preparations for wickedness! Hell itself would be tolerable if the upholsterers of Orleans had charge of it.

The duke spoke softly, then warmly, then magnificently. He promised estates, titles, jewels, protection, pleasures fine enough to make angels forsake their clouds. He knelt; he jested; he sighed; he swore. He painted delight as a garden where every tree bore sugar, every fountain ran wine, every bird sang madrigals, and no serpent had ever studied theology. Bertha stood against the table, white but composed.

“Never, while I live.”

“Then do not live too stubbornly.”

At that she drew from beneath her girdle a little Italian stiletto, thin as an icicle and bright as an evil thought. She set the point against her breast.

“Come one pace nearer,” said she, “and my blood shall cry between you and God.”

Louis stopped.

He knew courage when he saw it. He had seen men charge pikes and horses leap flames, but there was in Bertha’s stillness something stronger than fury. For a moment shame touched him; unhappily it touched only as a swallow touches water, and flew away.

“Put up your bodkin,” said he. “I am not a village ravisher.”

“No. A village ravisher may be hanged.”

“You shall go free.”

“Open the door.”

He did so, bowing with mock humility. She passed him without a word.

Had the matter ended there, Louis might have been called a libertine checked by virtue, which is a black title written upon grey paper. But wounded vanity is lust wearing armour. He could forgive chastity more readily than contempt, refusal more readily than defeat, and the stiletto had pierced him though it never left Bertha’s hand.

He waited, smiled upon Raoul, promoted him in trifles, praised his horsemanship, sent toys to his children, and devised a revenge which only a courtier could have polished and only a devil could have invented.

Three months later Raoul was summoned to supper at a house belonging to the duke near the Porte Barbette. With him came Guillaume de Saveuse, Hutin de Vermeilles, young Colard de Mailly, and two other gentlemen whose names charity has blotted from my copy. The room was low, warm, and painted with vines. Upon the table stood capons stuffed with chestnuts, eels in pepper, lampreys in red wine, larks baked by the dozen, a boar’s head with gilded tusks, cheeses strong enough to confess their own sins, wafers, marchpane, pears, nuts, and bottles from Beaune, Auxerre, Cyprus, and places which geographers have since hidden out of respectability.

The duke resolved that no man should leave sober enough to distinguish his conscience from his appetite.

They drank to the king, the queen, Burgundy, Orleans, France, the ladies, absent friends, present fools, future victories, past debts, Saint Martin, Saint Venus, and the blessed inventor of corks. They sang. They diced. They told stories concerning abbesses, millers’ daughters, merchants’ wives, shepherdesses, bath women, actresses, pilgrims, laundresses, and certain noble ladies whose names were concealed so carefully that every hearer knew them.

Raoul drank less than the others.

“What, Hocquetonville!” cried Louis. “Art thou become a monk?”

“I have a wife who prefers me Christian.”

“A wife! There is the cork in every good bottle.”

“Mine keeps the wine from souring.”

The company groaned at this domestic sentiment as wolves might groan at a sermon upon mutton.

The duke filled Raoul’s cup himself.

“Drink. Thou art among friends.”

That phrase has ruined more men than open enmity.

Now, behind the tapestry at the eastern end of the supper room there was a narrow door. Beyond it lay a dark bedchamber, and in that chamber Bertha had been confined since afternoon. She had been seized while returning from the convent of the Celestines, hooded, carried by closed litter, and brought through the garden passage. The duke himself had visited her only long enough to explain enough of his purpose to make terror complete.

“You shall not be touched by a stranger,” said he. “Indeed, I provide you a gallant whom you have often favoured.”

“You are mad.”

“No, madame. I am just. You chose a husband above a prince; this night shall prove the excellence of your choice.”

When she understood, her knees failed her.

“You cannot!”

“A duke can do many things which a wise man would avoid.”

“I will cry out.”

“And proclaim before six drunken gentlemen that Raoul has entered a strange woman’s bed? Proclaim yourself the woman? Which tale will Paris believe—the prince’s or yours? Honour is fine glass, madame; once cracked, witnesses mend it badly.”

“I will tell Raoul.”

“Tell him, and he kills me or I kill him. Be silent, and he wakes ashamed of a common infidelity, never knowing whom he wronged. Choose: his life, or your relief.”

Then he left her in darkness.

She tried the door, the shutters, the panel behind the bed. All were fast. She searched for a weapon, but even the pins had been taken from her hair. She prayed—first calmly, then desperately, then with that wordless inward cry which perhaps reaches heaven more quickly than Latin. Through the wall came laughter, cups striking wood, boots scraping rushes, and the voice of her husband.

Imagine her torment if you can; if you can imagine it easily, examine your heart.

At supper the duke began to describe a woman hidden nearby: not noble, he said, but more accomplished than ten countesses; discreet as a tomb, soft as ermine, lively as a flame, and skilled in every article of love’s guild, from the first glance to the final benediction.

Saveuse demanded her price. Mailly demanded her age. Vermeilles demanded whether she had a sister.

“She asks no money,” said Louis. “She has seen one among us and desires him.”

At this every man straightened, sucked in his belly, adjusted his beard, and believed himself chosen. Such is masculine modesty.

“Who?” they cried.

The duke looked round, prolonged the silence, and laid his hand upon Raoul’s shoulder.

“Our married saint.”

The room burst into laughter.

Raoul shook his head.

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because I love my wife.”

“Thou needst not marry this one.”

“I have no hunger.”

“Then eat for courtesy.”

“I am no capon to be stuffed after supper.”

“Art afraid?”

This word, which should frighten only cowards, is commonly the leash by which fools are led. The others took it up.

“Raoul is afraid!”

“Bertha keeps his courage in her workbasket!”

“He must ask leave of his nurse!”

Raoul flushed. He had drunk enough to feel insult more sharply than duty, yet not enough to lose all shame.

“My lord, command me against Burgundians, Englishmen, bandits, or boars. In this, excuse me.”

Louis smiled and poured another cup.

“I command nothing. I offer paradise. Refuse, and we shall know that marriage has made a hermit of the best lance in Valois.”

They teased, praised, challenged, embraced, and drowned him by drops. Wine spoke where friendship should have warned. At last Raoul rose unsteadily.

“One moment only,” said he, “to silence you muckworms.”

“Ha! Ha! Ha!” cried the duke. “The saint performs a miracle!”

Behind the wall Bertha heard the chair fall backward.

The hidden door opened. Raoul entered the unlighted chamber, and Louis locked it after him.

What passed there shall not be ornamented. There are jests which become crimes when pursued beyond the table, and curiosities which dishonour him who satisfies them. Raoul, clouded by wine, believing himself admitted to a courtesan’s chamber, did not know the silent woman who trembled beneath his touch. Bertha dared not speak; for the duke’s threat stood before her like an executioner, and her husband’s life seemed to hang upon her voice. She endured that which, between loving spouses, should have been tenderness, but which deceit transformed into humiliation and horror.

When Raoul had gone, confused, half-ashamed, and boasting falsely to hide his shame, the duke entered carrying a candle.

Bertha sat upon the edge of the bed. Her loosened hair covered her face. She appeared neither furious nor weeping, and this frightened Louis more than the stiletto had done.

“Well, madame,” said he, though his wit sounded thin, “you see I kept my promise. No stranger.”

She raised her head.

“You have made my husband betray me without knowledge, and me betray him through fear. You have put poison into what was pure. Listen now, Louis of Orleans. This chamber will follow you. It will walk behind your horse, sit beneath your council table, lie down beside your pleasures, and stand at last between you and mercy. You have not conquered me. You have destroyed something which you cannot restore, and the price will be paid by you, by him, and by me.”

The duke tried to laugh.

“Prophecies are women’s arrows; they fly far and strike nothing.”

“This one will strike.”

He let her leave through the garden gate before dawn.

Raoul returned home late the next day, sick in body and uneasy in spirit. Bertha received him with her accustomed gentleness, but when he kissed her brow she shuddered. He believed his drunken infidelity had somehow been discovered. He confessed that he had been led into folly, though he spared the details, and begged forgiveness.

She looked at him for a long while.

“You were deceived,” she said.

“That does not make me innocent.”

“No. But it makes another more guilty.”

She forgave him; yet from that day she changed. Not in affection—for she loved him more sorrowfully than before—but as a flower changes when deprived of air and eaten secretly by a worm. She grew pale. Music troubled her. Laughter heard through a wall made her tremble. She avoided dark rooms and could not endure the smell of cinnamon wine.

Raoul, seeing this, questioned her. For months she denied illness of the heart; but truth, like a spring beneath stones, finds at last some crevice. When the duke sent again for Raoul to attend him, Bertha clung to her husband and cried:

“Serve Burgundy, serve the king, serve the poorest knight in France, but serve that man no longer!”

Then all came out—not neatly, not in the order chroniclers prefer, but with tears, broken phrases, pauses, and the dreadful repetition of details which the injured soul cannot cease touching. Raoul listened standing. Once he gripped the table so strongly that the oak split at the edge. Once he asked, “Was it I?” and when she answered yes, he made a sound which she remembered until death.

He did not reproach her.

“Thou didst save my life,” he said.

“I lost mine.”

“No. He took it; and I will collect the debt.”

Shortly afterward Raoul quitted Orleans and entered the service of John, Duke of Burgundy. Some say he revealed everything to his new master; others that Burgundy knew only that Raoul bore Louis a mortal hatred and considered that recommendation sufficient. Princes are not overcurious concerning the griefs which furnish them useful swords.

On the twenty-third day of November in the year fourteen hundred and seven, Louis of Orleans supped with Queen Isabeau and afterward rode from the Hôtel Barbette. The night was cold; torches smoked in the mist; the horses’ shoes rang upon the street. Near the old gate, armed men rushed from concealment. “Death! Death!” they cried, in the Burgundian fashion.

Louis raised his arm.

“I am the Duke of Orleans!”

“That is why,” answered a voice.

Raoul d’Hocquetonville stepped from the shadow with a knotted club of applewood, bound at the head with iron. He might have used a sword, which is the weapon of gentlemen, but chose the club, saying afterward that villainy should be beaten like a rabid dog. He struck once upon the duke’s shoulder, once upon his temple, and a third time after Louis had fallen.

Whether Bertha’s prophecy stood visibly at the corner, I cannot say. But the duke died in the mud, his rings bright, his cloak rich, his blood black beneath the torches; and all the palaces, poets, perfumers, pages, flatterers, astrologers, hounds, hawks, lutes, velvets, and sugared quinces in France could not purchase him one further breath.

Raoul escaped to Burgundy’s protection. He lived, but not happily. Within the year Bertha died at Hocquetonville, being not yet thirty years of age. The physician wrote “decline of the lungs”; the priest wrote “God’s will”; her husband said nothing. She was buried beneath a plain stone bearing these words:

**HERE RESTS BERTHA, TRUE WIFE OF RAOUL,  
WHOM FALSEHOOD WOUNDED AND HEAVEN RECEIVED.**

Raoul caused no name to be added, for he said hers was enough. Each year, upon the day of her death, he laid upon the tomb a branch of white hawthorn. He never married again. In battle he was fierce, at feasts silent, and whenever men laughed too loudly over wine he would rise and leave them.

The Duke of Burgundy, passing the tomb some years later, read the inscription and remained thoughtful.

“Two honourable people,” said he, “were broken to feed one prince’s appetite.”

“My lord,” replied his chaplain, “and the prince was broken afterward.”

“That is justice.”

“Late justice.”

“All justice is late,” said Burgundy, “or men would call it prevention.”

Thus ended the affair of the dark chamber, which began with a glance at Christmas and concluded with a body in the Rue Vieille-du-Temple, a widow’s grave, and a husband who outlived his happiness. Let young lords who imagine power to be permission remember Louis; let companions who pour wine upon another man’s conscience remember Raoul; and let those who call steadfast women cold remember Bertha, who defended her honour first with reason, next with steel, and last with silence—though silence proved the cruellest weapon turned against herself.

As for the old saying that there is a woman at the bottom of everything, it was doubtless invented by a man standing at the top and pushing her down. In this business there was indeed a woman at the bottom: buried there. But above her stood appetite, mockery, wine, cowardly laughter, and the abused privilege of a prince.

Folly prepares the banquet, wickedness locks the door, and vengeance, though she arrives after the candles have guttered, never forgets the house.

### The Cartographer of Lost Roads

On the morning the road disappeared, Mara Venn was repairing a map of the northern marshes.

The map lay beneath a sheet of glass in her workshop, its paper yellowed to the color of old teeth. A century earlier, some patient hand had drawn every stream, footpath, and boundary stone in dark green ink. Time had eaten several holes through the marsh, and Mara was filling them with paper so thin it trembled when she breathed.

Outside, the village bell rang seven times.

Then it rang an eighth.

Mara lifted her head.

The bell keeper never made mistakes. He was eighty-six and nearly blind, but he measured time with the precision of a pendulum. An eighth bell at dawn meant only one thing: someone was missing.

She covered the map and went outside.

Half the village had already gathered in the square. Bakers stood with flour on their sleeves. Children clung to their mothers. A fisherman still carried a dripping net over one shoulder.

At the center of the crowd stood Mayor Pell, holding a lantern though the sun was up.

“It’s the east road,” he said when Mara approached.

“What about it?”

“It’s gone.”

The villagers parted to let her pass.

Mara walked to the edge of the square, beyond the blacksmith’s shop and the row of lime trees. The east road had always begun there. It ran between two low stone walls, crossed the barley fields, and continued toward the city of Orra, two days away.

Now the road ended at the last house.

Beyond it lay uninterrupted grass, silver with dew.

Mara stepped closer. There were no wheel ruts, no milestones, no walls. Even the drainage ditch had vanished. The meadow rolled toward the horizon as though no road had ever crossed it.

“Who’s missing?” she asked.

Mayor Pell lowered the lantern. “Tomas Reed. He left before dawn with a cart of apples. His wife watched him take the east road. Ten minutes later, she looked again, and there was only grass.”

A murmur moved through the crowd.

Mara knelt and touched the ground. The grass was cool and rooted deeply. It could not have grown in ten minutes. Near her boot, a line of ants marched through the soil without interruption.

“Bring me the village map,” she said.

No one moved.

“You’re the mapmaker,” said the mayor.

“Bring me the official map from the council hall.”

A boy ran to fetch it.

Mara had been called a mapmaker since inheriting her father’s workshop, though most of her work involved repairing documents made by the dead. She mended trade charts, estate plans, and sea maps whose monsters had faded to pale stains. She had drawn only one new map in her life: a plan of the village cemetery, commissioned after the gravedigger misplaced an aunt.

The boy returned carrying a wooden frame. Inside it was a map of the village and the lands surrounding it.

The east road was not there.

Mara stared at the blank space where the black line should have been.

“That’s impossible,” Mayor Pell whispered.

She removed the map from its frame and held it to the light. The road had not been erased. Erasure left scars: disturbed fibers, pale abrasions, crumbs of ink at the edges. This paper was smooth. The fields had been painted as one unbroken wash of green.

“Fetch every map you can find,” Mara said.

They brought maps from the schoolhouse, the inn, and the tax office. They brought a child’s hand-drawn treasure map and an embroidered county map from the wall of the baker’s parlor.

On every one, the east road had vanished.

Only Mara’s memory insisted it had existed.

By noon, a search party had crossed the meadow. They found no sign of Tomas, his horse, or his apples. They walked until they reached the low hills where the road should have bent south, but there was nothing except heather and stone.

Mara returned to her workshop and locked the door.

The northern marsh map still rested under glass. She removed it carefully and searched its eastern edge. There, scarcely wider than a thread, ran the old road to Orra.

She nearly laughed with relief.

This map was more than a hundred years old, drawn before the village had built its council hall. Whatever had altered the newer maps had missed it.

She followed the road with her finger. From the village it crossed the fields, climbed the low hills, passed through the Forest of Elms, and arrived at Orra’s western gate.

Halfway through the forest, the ink changed.

For most of its length, the road was green-black and precise. But in the forest it became a trembling gray line, faint as smoke. Beside it, written in a cramped hand, were four words:

ROAD CLOSED BY AGREEMENT.

Mara had repaired the map many times and never noticed the inscription.

She went to the cabinet where her father had kept his private papers. He had been dead eleven years, but the drawers still smelled faintly of tobacco and cedar oil. Receipts filled the first drawer. The second held letters tied in bundles. In the third, beneath a broken compass, she found a narrow ledger covered in blue leather.

Most of it recorded ordinary work.

Repaired Captain Harl’s coastal chart.  
Added new well south of chapel.  
Removed mill path after flood.

Then, near the final pages, she found an entry without a date.

A map is not a picture of the world. It is a promise the world has made.

Below it, another line had been written so heavily that the pen had torn the paper.

Promises can be broken.

Someone knocked.

Mara closed the ledger. “Who is it?”

“Eli.”

She opened the door.

Eli Reed was Tomas’s younger brother, a broad-shouldered man with rain-colored eyes. He carried his boots in one hand. Mud covered his trousers to the knees.

“I searched the hills,” he said. “Nothing.”

“I may know where the road went.”

“Then we’ll bring it back.”

She almost told him it was not so simple, but she had no idea whether that was true.

Mara packed the old map, her father’s ledger, ink, pens, a knife, food, rope, and a small brass compass. Eli brought two lanterns and an axe. Before sunset, they set out across the meadow.

The village watched in silence.

Mara navigated by the old map. Although the road was invisible, certain landmarks remained: a split boulder, a stream shaped like a hook, three ancient oaks on a ridge. By dusk, they reached the low hills.

There they found the first apple.

It lay in the grass, bright red and unbruised.

Eli picked it up. Ahead of them, another apple rested beneath a thornbush. Beyond that lay a third.

“Tomas is leaving a trail,” he said.

“Or the cart overturned.”

They followed the apples east.

Night came quickly. Clouds swallowed the moon, and their lanterns cast small, uncertain circles over the ground. The apples led them into the Forest of Elms.

The trees stood close together, their branches woven overhead. No wind stirred, yet the leaves whispered continuously. Mara checked the compass. Its needle spun once, stopped pointing west, then sank as if exhausted.

They continued by the map.

After an hour, the apple trail ended at a stone arch.

It stood alone among the trees, twice Mara’s height, built from blocks furred with moss. There was no wall around it, no ruin, nothing to explain why it existed.

Within the archway, rain was falling.

On Mara’s side the night remained dry, but beyond the stones she saw rain slanting across a pale road. Wheel tracks shone in the mud.

Eli stepped forward.

Mara caught his arm. “Wait.”

On the arch’s left pillar, hidden beneath lichen, someone had carved a symbol: a circle divided by four roads. She had seen it in her father’s ledger, sketched beside the words ROAD CLOSED BY AGREEMENT.

“What agreement?” Eli asked.

“I don’t know.”

“Tomas is through there.”

“Maybe.”

“That’s his cart track.”

Before Mara could stop him, Eli crossed the threshold.

He did not vanish. He stood on the other side in the rain, turned, and held out his hand.

She followed.

Cold water struck her face. When she looked back, the forest beyond the arch was sunlit.

Not dawn-lit. Sunlit.

Birds sang among green leaves. Through the doorway, it appeared to be midday in another season.

Eli stared.

“Don’t try to understand it yet,” Mara said. “We’ll only waste time.”

The road stretched ahead, pale beneath the rain. It was bordered by leaning milestones, each carved with a number that changed when Mara looked away. One read 17, then 42, then 3.

They walked.

The forest on either side was wrong. Pines grew beside flowering cherries. Autumn leaves covered summer ferns. Once they passed a frozen pond with dragonflies hovering above it. Another time they heard children laughing among the trees, though no children appeared.

At last they saw the cart.

It stood crooked in the road, one wheel sunk in mud. Apples filled the back. The horse was gone.

“Tomas!” Eli shouted.

A figure emerged from behind the cart.

Tomas looked unharmed, but his beard had grown to his chest.

Eli stopped as if struck.

Tomas raised his lantern. His face crumpled.

“You came,” he said.

They embraced in the middle of the road. Tomas clung to his brother with both arms.

“How long?” Mara asked.

“Six months,” he replied.

“You left this morning.”

“For you, perhaps.”

He had survived on apples and water from the rain. Whenever he tried to leave the road, the forest turned him around. If he walked east, he returned to his cart from the west. If he walked west, he came back from the east.

“And there’s something else,” he said. “Something comes at midnight.”

A bell rang in the distance.

One clear note.

Tomas went pale. “We have to hide.”

“From what?”

“The collector.”

He dragged them behind the cart and pulled a rotting canvas over their heads. Mara crouched between the apple crates, listening.

The bell rang again.

Hoofbeats approached, slow and measured.

Through a tear in the canvas, Mara saw a rider coming down the road.

The rider wore a long white coat buttoned to the throat. Its horse was black, but not the black of fur or ink. It was the black of a doorway at night, a black that seemed cut out of the world.

When the rider reached the cart, it stopped.

“Three travelers,” it said.

Its voice sounded like paper being folded.

No one answered.

The canvas lifted by itself.

The rider had no face. Beneath the brim of its hat was a smooth oval of parchment crossed with fine blue lines. Roads. Rivers. Borders. As Mara watched, the lines shifted.

“A Venn,” the rider said. “At last.”

Eli raised his axe, but Mara caught the handle.

“You know my name?”

“I knew your father.”

The rider dismounted. It unfolded until it stood unnaturally tall.

“Your father was the keeper of this road,” it said. “He maintained the agreement between your village and the old ways. When he died, no successor came.”

“He never told me.”

“He hoped silence would free you. Silence frees no one from a promise.”

Mara thought of the ledger hidden inside her coat.

“What was the agreement?”

The rider turned its blank, mapped face toward her. “Long ago, your village was built where many roads crossed. Not roads of stone. Roads of possibility. The dead walked one. The unborn walked another. Lost armies came marching through summer fields. Winter arrived in June. Your people begged for safety.”

“So a mapmaker closed the roads,” Mara said.

“A Venn drew boundaries. We honored them. In return, one road remained open, and one member of your family tended it.”

“Then why did the east road disappear?”

“Because no road remains where its promise is neglected. It has fallen out of your world and into mine.”

“And Tomas?”

“A traveler must belong somewhere. When the road was forgotten, it brought him with it.”

Eli stepped forward. “Send us home.”

“I cannot.”

The rain clicked softly against the apple crates.

Mara looked at the rider’s face. One of the moving lines resembled the coast north of Orra. Another curled like the river beside her village.

“What are you collecting?” she asked.

“Unkept promises.”

“And what happens when you collect this one?”

“The road closes completely. What it carries remains here.”

“All three of us?”

“All who have entered.”

Mara’s hand tightened around her father’s ledger. “There must be a way to restore it.”

“A keeper may redraw the road.”

“Then give me ink.”

“You carry ink.”

“Ordinary ink can’t change the world.”

The rider tilted its head. “All ink is ordinary until someone believes the line.”

From its coat, it produced a rolled sheet of paper and gave it to her.

The paper was warm.

Mara unrolled it across an apple crate. A map appeared on its surface: her village in exquisite detail. She saw the square, the chapel, her workshop, and even the cracked rain barrel behind it. But east of the village there was nothing. The paper simply ended in whiteness.

“Draw the road,” said the collector.

Mara took out her pen and ink. Her hand hovered over the map.

It seemed easy. A single line from the village to Orra. Yet she remembered her father’s warning: A map is a promise the world has made.

“What is the cost?”

The collector stood motionless.

“There is always a cost,” she said.

“To draw a road is to accept where it leads.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only answer.”

Tomas gripped the side of the cart to steady himself. Eli watched Mara, waiting.

She put the pen down.

“My father kept this road, didn’t he? Not by repairing maps in his workshop. By coming here.”

“Yes.”

“How often?”

“At the first snow of every year.”

Mara remembered those journeys. Her father used to vanish for three or four days each winter, claiming he was inspecting boundary markers. He always returned tired. As a child, she had searched his pockets for gifts and found only stones, dead leaves, and once a silver coin stamped with the face of an unknown queen.

“If I redraw it, I become the keeper.”

“Yes.”

“And when I die?”

“The road will require another promise.”

She thought of generations of Venns passing this burden from parent to child, each one guarding the village without being able to explain why. Perhaps her father had wanted the chain to end. Perhaps he had believed the road would quietly fade.

Instead, it had taken an innocent traveler.

Mara dipped her pen.

The first mark spread across the page like a root through soil. Somewhere in the distance, stone cracked.

She drew east from the village.

The road appeared beneath their feet, its edges sharpening. Mud became fitted stone. Drainage ditches opened on either side. The leaning milestones straightened.

She continued the line through the hills and into the forest.

The trees shuddered. Seasons peeled apart. Snow vanished from the ferns, blossoms fell from the pines, and the air settled into late summer.

When the line reached the place where they stood, the pen stopped.

Not because Mara stopped it. The nib would go no farther.

The collector watched.

“To accept where it leads,” Mara whispered.

She looked beyond the unfinished ink. If she followed the old map, the road would continue to Orra. But the old map had failed. It had hidden the arch, the shifting forest, and the place beneath the rain. It described only one version of the world.

Mara turned the pen back toward the village.

“What are you doing?” Eli asked.

“Making a road home.”

She drew a second line parallel to the first, then joined them. Not a single path, but a road with two directions.

The paper trembled.

The collector seized her wrist. Its fingers were cold and flat.

“That is not the agreement.”

“No,” Mara said. “It’s a new one.”

“You cannot bargain with the old ways.”

“Every boundary is a bargain.”

The lines on the collector’s face twisted into a storm. The black horse screamed.

Mara pulled free and drew.

She added the stone arch and marked it as a gate. She drew the path through the meadow, the square, and the door of her workshop. Beside the road she wrote:

NO TRAVELER SHALL BE KEPT AGAINST THEIR WILL.

The collector bent over the words. Rain poured from the brim of its hat.

“A map cannot command what it does not understand,” it said.

“Neither can a keeper honor an agreement she was never allowed to know.”

The road shook. Apples bounced from the cart and rolled over the stones.

“What do you offer?” asked the collector.

Mara knew then that she had been right. The old ways were not kings. They were traders.

“Once every year, I will come to the gate,” she said. “I will repair the boundaries and record what has changed. The road may remain between worlds, but any lost traveler will be shown the way home.”

“And when travelers enter willingly?”

“They may pass.”

“What payment will they make?”

“Stories.”

The collector became very still.

Mara sensed Eli’s confusion, but she continued.

“Every traveler who uses the hidden road will leave a true story at the gate. In return, the road will carry them where they need to go—not where they wish to go, but where they need to.”

The blank face bent closer.

“Stories fade.”

“So do roads.”

“Stories change.”

“So do maps.”

For the first time, the collector seemed to laugh. The sound was like a thousand pages turning at once.

“Draw it,” it said.

Mara wrote the agreement in the margin. The words glowed briefly, then sank into the paper.

At once, the rain stopped.

The forest became quiet.

The collector mounted its horse. “The road has accepted you, Mara Venn.”

“I haven’t accepted it.”

“You drew the line.”

It turned the horse eastward.

“What happened to my father?” Mara called.

The collector paused.

“He tried to erase the road,” it said. “But erasure is not destruction. It is only a mark someone refuses to see.”

Then horse and rider folded into the distance, growing thinner until they became a dark line on the horizon.

Mara completed the road to the edge of the paper.

The archway appeared ahead, sunlight shining through it.

Tomas’s horse waited on the other side, calmly eating grass.

They pushed the cart through just after dawn.

Only one night had passed in the village, though Tomas had aged half a year. His wife ran across the meadow and struck him once before embracing him. The villagers gathered around, shouting questions, touching the cart and the horse as if to make sure they were real.

Behind them, the east road had returned.

It curved between two low stone walls, crossed the barley fields, and climbed toward the hills. The first milestone stood beneath an elm, clean and white.

Mayor Pell found Mara at the edge of the crowd.

“What happened?” he asked.

She looked at the faces around her. They deserved the truth, yet the truth was too large to give them all at once.

“The road was neglected,” she said. “I repaired it.”

That evening, she returned to her workshop and examined every map.

The east road had reappeared on all of them, but each map now included a small stone arch in the Forest of Elms. Beside it was a symbol: a circle divided by four roads.

Mara hung the oldest map above her desk.

Over the following months, travelers began to arrive.

Some came from Orra and other familiar places. Others did not. A woman in bronze armor appeared one morning, carrying a broken spear and speaking a language that had not been heard for nine hundred years. A boy came looking for a city that would not be built until long after Mara’s death. An old man arrived from a country where people kept sunlight in glass jars.

Each traveler left a story.

Mara wrote them all in blue ledgers.

When the first snow fell, she packed food, ink, and blank paper. Eli went with her, though she told him he did not have to. Tomas stayed home. He never traveled east again, but every autumn he left a basket of apples beside the first milestone.

At the stone arch, Mara found the collector waiting.

It stood beside its black horse, white coat bright against the snow. The shifting lines on its face showed roads she had never seen.

“Keeper,” it said.

“Collector.”

Between them stood a wooden box that had not been there before.

Inside were hundreds of folded papers. Each held a story, written in a different hand.

Mara took out the first.

It began:

On the morning the road disappeared, Mara Venn was repairing a map of the northern marshes.

She looked up sharply.

The collector’s paper face revealed nothing.

“Who wrote this?”

“A traveler.”

“From where?”

“From a place where your road has already ended.”

Mara read the sentence again. Then she folded the paper and returned it to the box.

“Does it end well?” Eli asked.

“All roads end,” said the collector.

Mara opened her ink bottle and spread a fresh map over the snow.

“Not today,” she said.

Then she began to draw.
